name: Cufet
_readme: There is deliberately no $schema here. The only TextMate grammar schema in circulation is
a third-party file on raw.githubusercontent.com, which VS Code refuses to fetch unless you
add the domain to json.schemaDownload trusted locations — so referencing it shows everyone
who opens this file a warning, in exchange for nothing at load time: the grammar loader
ignores $schema. Add it back locally if you want completions while editing.
A TextMate grammar assigns SCOPES; the colour theme maps scopes to colours. So this file
names scopes from the standard vocabulary every theme already styles, and never picks a
colour. Scope names are three-part — <standard-prefix>.<cufet-role>.cufet — so a plain
theme colours them by the prefix it already knows, and a theme with a wide palette can
pull the Cufet-specific roles apart if it wants to.
THE ONE RULE THAT MATTERS: articles and prepositions get NO scope. 'a', 'an', 'the', 'of',
plain body text. Cufet reads as English because it is full of them, and colouring them
would turn every line into a wall of keyword. Unscoped, they recede and the content words
carry the line. This is deliberate. Do not 'fix' it.
WORD BOUNDARIES: \b is wrong here. Hyphens are identifier characters in Cufet, so 'add-edge'
is ONE name — but \b sees a boundary at the hyphen and would colour the 'add' in it as a
keyword. Every keyword pattern below is fenced with (?<![\w-]) ... (?![\w-]) instead.
Keywords are case-insensitive in the lexer, hence (?i:...) throughout.

line-comment.comment: Matched BEFORE #comment so that a '/*' appearing inside a // comment does not open a block. Runs to end of line; nothing inside it is scoped further.
line-comment.name: comment.line.double-slash.cufet

comment.comment: Cufet block comments nest — an inner /* must be closed before the outer one ends. The self-include is what implements that, and it is the whole reason commenting out a block that already contains comments works. Rust and Swift nest theirs the same way.
comment.name: comment.block.cufet

patterns.comment: \{ and \} are literal braces, NOT interpolation — so they must be taken before #interpolation gets a look.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.cufet

patterns.comment: The lexer rejects any other escape outright, so flagging it here is accurate, not a guess.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unknown-escape.cufet

interpolation.comment: A hole holds a full expression, including nested strings with holes of their own — hence $self.
interpolation.name: meta.interpolation.cufet

patterns.comment: Bit patterns: 0x hex, 0b binary, 0o octal, with '_' grouping digits. Must come before the decimal rule, which would otherwise match the leading 0, fail its right fence against the base letter, and leave 'xFF' to be read as an identifier. No bare-0 octal, so 0755 stays decimal and falls through to the rule below.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.bits.cufet

patterns.comment: A '-' hard against a digit, with no word character in front of it. The left fence is what separates this from 'batch-1', where the '-' follows a letter and the whole thing is one identifier. Scoped as operator-plus-number rather than one numeric token, so it renders identically to the binary 'x - 1' — the parser, not the grammar, decides which it is, and the highlighting should not claim to know better.
Matches the lexer exactly: a '.' is a decimal point only when a digit follows it, so the '.' in 'State 3.' stays a statement terminator.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.cufet

patterns.comment: Bind <return type> to <name>. The return type may itself contain 'to' — 'Bind map from text to number to dijkstra' — so the middle is greedy and backtracks to the LAST 'to', which is the one that introduces the name. 'unto' is not caught by it, because the left fence rejects a preceding word character.
Define object <name> with (...)
Define <name> as an interface for {...} — here the name comes BEFORE the keyword that identifies the form, so the literal 'interface' is what keeps this off ordinary 'Define x as 1'.
a new <type> { ... }
Bind <ret> to <name> unto <type> — the method's owning type.
Cast <name> on (...). The article is optional and stays unscoped, like every other article.
Pull a book on <name> [as <alias>] / Pull books on <n>, <n>, and <n>. Both the book names and a local alias are namespace names, so one sub-pattern covers the tail.

accessor-phrase.comment: Cufet's positional and built-in-field accessors are CONTEXTUAL, not reserved — 'first', 'last' and 'value' are ordinary identifiers that the parser only recognises in a particular shape. Anchoring on the article in front of them reproduces that shape closely enough to colour them like the reserved accessors they sit beside, so 'the key of pair' and 'the value of pair' don't come out looking like two different things.

patterns.comment: read all / read line / read lines / read input — the form words are contextual too.

phrase.comment: Multi-word operators, coloured as a unit. These must run before the single-word keywords: colouring 'is greater' and leaving a plain 'than' hanging off the end looks broken, and 'for' on its own has no business being loud in 'open for reading'.

patterns.comment: 'matrix' is contextual — a type only where the mandatory 'with' follows it, exactly as the parser decides. Everywhere else it is an ordinary name and renders as one. The lookahead does not consume the 'with', which stays an unscoped preposition.

possessive.comment: The 's goes with the OWNER, not on its own. In English "one's" is one word — the genitive of "one" — and colouring the marker separately splits a word down the middle. A '.' between identifiers gets away with staying plain because it is a symbol and reads as a gap; 's contains a letter, so a differently-coloured 's welded to the end of a name just looks like the name lost its colour halfway through.

patterns.comment: The reserved pronouns keep their own scope through the marker.
After a closing paren — '(the first of pq)'s pq-dist' — there is no word to attach to, so here the marker really is standing on its own and is scoped as the operator it is.
Flow.
patterns.name: keyword.control.flow.cufet

patterns.comment: Statement verbs — the words that open a statement and say what it does. ★ 'output' and 'seed' are deliberately NOT in this list: they lex as identifiers, so a program may name a variable either one, and matching them case-insensitively here would repaint that variable as language syntax. The CAPITALISED spelling is handled by the rule below, and the lowercase one by the semantic-token pass.
patterns.name: keyword.control.statement.cufet

patterns.comment: Words that introduce a definition.
patterns.name: storage.type.declaration.cufet

patterns.comment: ★ 'Output' and 'Seed', CAPITALISED ONLY and matched case-sensitively. This rule cannot be wrong: an identifier must begin with a lowercase letter, so the capitalised spelling can only ever be the statement — it is never someone's variable. The lowercase spelling IS ambiguous and is left to the semantic-token pass, which has the parse and can tell a statement from a variable of the same name (see SemanticTokenKind.Keyword). Keeping both layers is deliberate: semantic tokens are unavailable whenever a file does not parse, and this guarantees the capitalised form is coloured regardless.
patterns.name: keyword.control.statement.cufet

patterns.comment: Type names. 'text', 'fact' and 'bits' are contextual rather than reserved — the lexer has no token for any of them — but they are types to anyone reading the code, so they are coloured as types.
patterns.name: support.type.cufet

patterns.comment: Word-form operators.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.word.cufet

patterns.comment: Built-in accessors and nouns.
patterns.name: support.function.builtin.cufet

patterns.comment: 'it' is the last stated value; 'one' is the self-reference inside a method body. Both are the language handing you a name, which is what variable.language means.
patterns.name: variable.language.cufet

patterns.comment: Binary '-' needs spaces around it, because a hyphen with a letter or digit after it is part of an identifier: 'count-1' is one name, 'count - 1' is subtraction. The identifier pattern is not scoped, so the two really do render differently — which is the point.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.arithmetic.cufet

patterns.comment: The streaming pipe: A | B wires A's output to B's input.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.pipe.cufet

function-word.comment: Articles and prepositions, matched WITH NO NAME so they are consumed and left unscoped. This rule earns its place by running before #identifier: without it the catch-all below would claim 'the' and 'of' as variables and light up every line, which is the exact outcome the no-scope-for-function-words rule exists to prevent. Words that also carry structural weight ('unto', 'but', 'not') are keywords and are claimed earlier.

identifier.comment: Everything still standing is a name the author chose — locals, parameters, fields, arguments. Scoping them matters more in Cufet than in a symbol-heavy language: strip the articles and prepositions out of a line and most of what remains IS an identifier, so leaving them at default foreground is what makes a Cufet file read flatter than the C# next to it. Themes give variable.other its own colour.
identifier.name: variable.other.cufet
